concepts.title: Helm Charts and Templating
concepts.description: Helm packages a set of related Kubernetes manifests into a single, versioned, parameterized chart -- Go templating over a values.yaml file lets one chart definition render differently for dev, staging, and production, replacing what would otherwise be dozens of hand-maintained, drifting near-duplicate YAML files.
learningObjectives: Explain the specific maintenance problems that emerge when raw YAML manifests are hand-duplicated across multiple services and environments.
Describe a Helm chart's directory structure and the role of Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and the templates/ directory.
Use Go template syntax ({{ .Values.x }}, {{ .Release.Name }}, conditionals, ranges, pipelines) to parameterize a manifest.
Explain how values.yaml defaults are overridden at install/upgrade time via -f and --set, and the precedence order between them.
Use helm template and helm lint to inspect a chart's fully rendered output before it ever reaches the cluster.
Predict and fix a common templating bug caused by multi-line values breaking YAML indentation when rendered.

sections.heading: Why Raw YAML Stops Scaling
sections.body:
A single Deployment-plus-Service pair is easy to hand-write and hand-edit. The trouble starts multiplying: once you have N services, each needing to run in M environments (dev, staging, prod, maybe a per-developer sandbox), you're suddenly maintaining something close to N times M near-duplicate YAML files, differing from each other only in a handful of values -- an image tag, a replica count, a resource limit, an environment variable pointing at a different database host. Nothing about plain YAML gives you a mechanism to say 'these 40 files are really the same template with different parameters' -- they're just 40 independent files that happen to look similar today.

The practical failure mode is drift: someone bumps the memory limit in the production Deployment during an incident and forgets to make the same change in staging; a new label gets added to 12 of the 20 copies because the other 8 were edited by someone who didn't know to add it. Worse, there's no single version number for 'this exact bundle of manifests, as deployed to production last Tuesday' -- if you want to know what changed between two deploys, you're diffing raw files by hand, and if you want to roll back, you're manually reverting each file and hoping you didn't miss one. Helm's answer is to stop treating each environment's manifests as independent files at all, and instead treat them as one parameterized template rendered differently per environment, with the specific set of parameter values captured and versioned as a first-class artifact.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Chart
sections.body:
A Helm chart is a directory with a fixed, conventional structure:

```text
my-app/
├── Chart.yaml          # chart metadata: name, version, appVersion
├── values.yaml         # default configuration values
├── charts/             # bundled sub-charts (dependencies), if any
└── templates/
    ├── deployment.yaml  # Go-template-annotated Kubernetes manifests
    ├── service.yaml
    ├── _helpers.tpl     # reusable named template snippets
    └── NOTES.txt        # post-install usage text shown to the user
```

`Chart.yaml` carries the chart's own identity: its `name`, its own semantic `version` (how many times this chart's packaging has changed), and separately `appVersion` (the version of the actual application it deploys -- these two version numbers are deliberately independent, since you can ship a packaging fix without the application itself changing at all, or vice versa). `values.yaml` holds the chart author's chosen defaults for every parameter the templates reference. Everything under `templates/` is not, by itself, valid Kubernetes YAML -- it's Go template *source*, containing `{{ }}` placeholders that only become real YAML once Helm renders them by substituting in actual values. `_helpers.tpl` is where reusable snippets live (a standard label block, a computed name, anything referenced from multiple templates via `{{ include "my-app.labels" . }}`), so you're not repeating the same boilerplate across every file under `templates/`.

sections.heading: Templating with Go Templates: Values, Objects, and Control Flow
sections.body:
Inside a template file, `{{ .Values.image.tag }}` reaches into the merged values data (covered fully in the next section) and substitutes whatever `image.tag` resolves to. A handful of other built-in objects are available alongside `.Values`: `.Release.Name` and `.Release.Namespace` (the specific release being installed -- covered in the next concept), and `.Chart.Name`/`.Chart.Version` (metadata pulled straight from Chart.yaml).

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount | default 1 }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          {{- if .Values.resources }}
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
          {{- end }}
```

`| default 1` is a **pipeline**: it feeds `.Values.replicaCount` into the `default` function, which substitutes `1` only if the value is empty or unset -- a defensive fallback independent of whatever's in `values.yaml`. `{{- if .Values.resources }} ... {{- end }}` is a conditional block that only emits the enclosed YAML at all if `resources` is actually set, which matters because emitting an empty `resources: {}` block is harmless but emitting a `resources:` key with nothing under it can produce invalid YAML depending on what follows. `{{- range .Values.env }} ... {{- end }}` (not shown above) is the looping construct, used for anything list-shaped, such as a variable number of environment variables. The leading `{{-` and trailing `-}}` (rather than plain `{{`/`}}`) are whitespace-trim markers: they strip the newline and indentation immediately before/after the tag, which is what keeps rendered output from accumulating stray blank lines every time a conditional or loop is used -- a purely cosmetic-looking detail that actually determines whether the rendered file is even valid YAML, since stray blank lines inside a block scalar can shift indentation in ways that break parsing.

sections.heading: Overriding Defaults: values.yaml Precedence
sections.body:
`values.yaml` inside the chart supplies the chart author's defaults, but almost nobody deploys a chart using only those defaults for every environment. Helm supports layering values from multiple sources, and the precedence order -- highest wins -- is: `--set` flags on the command line, then `-f`/`--values` files in the order given (later files override earlier ones), then the chart's own bundled `values.yaml` as the final fallback.

```bash
helm install web ./my-app \
  -f values-prod.yaml \
  --set replicaCount=5 \
  --set image.tag=2.3.1
```

Merging is a **deep merge** on maps, not a wholesale replacement: if the chart's `values.yaml` defines `resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } }` and `values-prod.yaml` only overrides `resources.requests.memory: 512Mi`, the resulting merged value keeps `cpu: 100m` from the default and only changes `memory`. This lets an environment-specific values file stay small, listing only what actually differs, rather than having to restate every key.

Before ever running `helm install` or `helm upgrade` against a real cluster, `helm template ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` renders the exact same output locally, with zero cluster interaction -- printing the final YAML that would be sent to the API server, so you can read it, diff it against a previous render, or pipe it into `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -` for an extra validation pass. `helm lint ./my-app` runs a separate set of structural checks (missing required values, YAML that won't parse, obviously malformed chart metadata) and is the first thing worth running after editing any template, since it catches a large class of mistakes before you even get to rendering.

sections.heading: The Multi-Line Indentation Trap
sections.body:
One specific templating mistake shows up constantly, precisely because it looks correct until you actually render it: embedding a multi-line value (a resources block, an arbitrary map of annotations, a whole config file's contents) using `toYaml` without accounting for indentation.

```yaml
# BROKEN: toYaml's own indentation doesn't match its surrounding context
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          resources:
{{ toYaml .Values.resources }}
```

`toYaml` serializes `.Values.resources` starting at column 0, with no awareness at all of how deeply nested it needs to sit inside the surrounding `containers:` block -- the raw substitution above produces a `resources:` key followed by content indented at column 0, which is invalid relative to a container list item several levels deep. The fix is `nindent`, which does two things at once: it inserts a newline before the content, and indents every line of that content by the given number of spaces:

```yaml
# FIXED
        - name: app
          resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
```

`nindent 12` places the rendered block at exactly 12 spaces of indentation, matching where a `resources:` value needs to sit under a container entry that itself starts at column 10 (`- name:`) plus its own field's 2-space step. Getting this number wrong by even one level produces YAML that's syntactically valid but semantically wrong (the block silently attaches to the wrong parent key), or outright invalid, which is exactly why `helm template` should always be run and its output actually read after touching any template that embeds a nested structure this way -- the bug is invisible in the template source itself and only appears in the rendered result.

examples.title: A Minimal Chart: values.yaml and a Parameterized Deployment
examples.code:
# values.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: my-registry/my-app
  tag: "1.4.0"
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi

---
# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
examples.explanation: Every field that could plausibly differ per environment or per release -- the replica count, the image tag, the resource requests -- is pulled from `.Values` instead of being hardcoded. `{{ .Release.Name }}` is used both for the Deployment's own name and for the Pod template's label, which means installing this chart twice under two different release names (e.g. `web-blue` and `web-green`) automatically produces two non-colliding, independently selectable sets of objects with zero changes to the template itself. Running `helm template ./my-app` with no overrides at all renders exactly this structure with `replicas: 2`, `image: "my-registry/my-app:1.4.0"`, and the resources block correctly nested -- that rendered output is genuinely just ordinary Kubernetes YAML by the time it reaches the API server; nothing template-specific survives into what actually gets applied.

examples.title: Overriding Values at Install Time
examples.code:
# Render with only the chart's own defaults -- no overrides
helm template web ./my-app | grep -A1 replicas
#   replicas: 2

# Render with a production values file plus a one-off --set override
helm template web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml --set replicaCount=5 | grep -A1 replicas
#   replicas: 5

# values-prod.yaml itself only sets:
# replicaCount: 3
# image:
#   tag: "1.4.0-prod"
examples.explanation: Even though `values-prod.yaml` sets `replicaCount: 3`, the final rendered output shows `replicas: 5` -- because `--set` sits above `-f` files in Helm's precedence order, regardless of the order the flags happen to appear on the command line. This is exactly the mechanism CI/CD pipelines rely on: a values file checked into the chart's repo captures the stable, reviewed configuration for an environment, while a `--set` flag layered on top handles a one-off, ad hoc override (a hotfix image tag, a temporary scale-up) without needing to edit and commit a file first. `helm template` here never touches a cluster at all -- it's purely a local rendering step, which is exactly why it's the right tool for checking precedence behavior like this before ever running `install` or `upgrade` for real.

examples.title: The nindent Bug, Broken and Fixed
examples.code:
# BROKEN -- toYaml's output isn't indented to match its context
containers:
  - name: app
    resources:
{{ toYaml .Values.resources }}
# Renders to:
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
# requests:
#   cpu: 100m
#   memory: 128Mi
# --  "requests" is at column 0, no longer nested under "resources" at all

# FIXED
containers:
  - name: app
    resources:
{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 6 }}
# Renders to:
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
#       requests:
#         cpu: 100m
#         memory: 128Mi
examples.explanation: In the broken version, `toYaml` serializes the `resources` map starting at column 0 because it has no idea it's being embedded six spaces deep -- the raw `{{ toYaml ... }}` substitution just drops that text in verbatim, indentation and all, wherever the template tag happens to sit. The result parses as YAML, but `requests` ends up as a top-level sibling of `containers` instead of a child of `resources`, which is a silent, structurally wrong render rather than an outright syntax error -- exactly the kind of bug that survives a casual glance and only shows up once you diff the rendered output or watch the applied object misbehave. `nindent 6` fixes this by prefixing every line of the serialized block with 6 spaces of indentation (and a leading newline), correctly nesting it as a child of `resources:` at the depth this specific template position requires. There's no way to know the right number to pass to `nindent` except by counting the indentation of the surrounding YAML by hand -- which is exactly why running `helm template` and reading the actual rendered output, rather than just trusting the template source, is the only reliable way to catch this class of mistake.

misconceptions.description: The values baked into a chart's own values.yaml are essentially fixed once the chart is written -- meaningfully changing behavior per environment requires forking or hand-editing the chart itself.
misconceptions.clarification: values.yaml only supplies the lowest-precedence defaults; it's specifically designed to be overridden without touching the chart at all, via one or more -f/--values files layered on top (later files win over earlier ones) and --set flags on the command line (which win over every file). A well-authored chart is written once and reused unmodified across every environment, with only the values changing -- forking the chart to change a value defeats the entire purpose of separating the template from its configuration.

misconceptions.description: A file under templates/ that looks like valid, complete Kubernetes YAML (aside from the {{ }} placeholders) could be applied directly with kubectl apply -f, since the {{ }} bits are just extra annotations Kubernetes would ignore.
misconceptions.clarification: Files under templates/ are Go template source, not Kubernetes manifests -- the {{ }} syntax has no meaning to the Kubernetes API server at all. Applying such a file directly would send literal text like `{{ .Values.replicaCount }}` as the value of a field expecting an integer, and the API server would reject it outright as malformed. Only Helm's own rendering step (invoked internally by helm install/upgrade, or explicitly via helm template) actually substitutes real values and produces genuine YAML -- nothing under templates/ is meant to be read by anything other than Helm's template engine first.

exercises.prompt: A chart's values.yaml sets `replicaCount: 2`. A team maintains `values-prod.yaml` with `replicaCount: 3`. Someone runs the command below during an incident to temporarily scale up. What replica count does the rendered Deployment actually have, and why?
hints: Three different sources define replicaCount here: the chart's own values.yaml, the -f file, and --set. List them out and think about which one Helm treats as authoritative when they conflict.
Precedence, from lowest to highest, is: the chart's own values.yaml, then -f files in the order given, then --set flags.
--set is specifically designed for exactly this situation -- a one-off override that should win over whatever a checked-in values file says, without needing to edit that file.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 10. --set sits at the highest precedence level, above any -f file and above the chart's own values.yaml, regardless of the order the flags appear on the command line -- so replicaCount=10 wins over both replicaCount: 3 (values-prod.yaml) and replicaCount: 2 (the chart's default).
exercises.solutionExplanation: Helm resolves conflicting values by a fixed precedence order, independent of the order flags are typed: --set (and --set-string/--set-file) always wins over any -f/--values file, which in turn always wins over the chart's own bundled values.yaml. Here, replicaCount is defined three times -- 2 in the chart's default values.yaml, 3 in values-prod.yaml, and 10 via --set -- and since --set is the highest-precedence source, the rendered Deployment ends up with replicas: 10. This is precisely why --set is the standard tool for a temporary, ad hoc override during an incident: it doesn't require editing or committing a change to values-prod.yaml at all, and its effect is scoped to just this one upgrade invocation.

exercises.prompt: This template is meant to attach a variable-length set of annotations from values.yaml onto a Deployment, but `helm template` produces YAML where the annotations end up as siblings of `metadata` instead of nested underneath it. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
# values.yaml
annotations:
  team: platform
  owner: sre

# templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  annotations:
{{ toYaml .Values.annotations }}
spec:
  replicas: 1
hints: toYaml serializes .Values.annotations starting at column 0 -- it has no awareness of how many spaces of indentation this specific spot in the template actually needs.
Compare the indentation of `annotations:` above the {{ }} line to the indentation `toYaml`'s raw output would need to land at to nest correctly underneath it.
There's a template function specifically built to indent every line of a multi-line block by a fixed number of spaces before inserting it.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
  annotations:
{{- toYaml .Values.annotations | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  replicas: 1
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `{{ toYaml .Values.annotations }}` drops the serialized map in verbatim at column 0, so `team: platform` and `owner: sre` end up aligned with `apiVersion`/`metadata`/`spec` -- structurally siblings of the whole Deployment's top-level keys, not children of `annotations`. Piping through `nindent 4` fixes this by indenting every line of the serialized block by 4 spaces (matching where a value under `metadata.annotations` needs to sit, since `annotations:` itself sits at 2 spaces and its children need one more 2-space step) and inserting a leading newline so the first annotation line doesn't get glued onto the same line as `annotations:`. The leading `{{-` also trims the newline/whitespace before the tag, keeping the render free of a stray blank line at that point.

assessments.prompt: A chart's values.yaml sets `image.tag: "1.0"`. You run `helm install web ./my-app -f values-a.yaml --set image.tag=2.0`, where values-a.yaml sets `image.tag: "1.5"`. What image tag ends up in the rendered manifest?
options: 1.0, because the chart's own values.yaml is always treated as the final source of truth.
1.5, because -f files are applied last, after --set flags are evaluated.
2.0, because --set has the highest precedence, overriding both the -f file and the chart's own values.yaml.
Helm raises an error because the same key is defined in three different places.
assessments.explanation: Helm's value precedence, from lowest to highest, is: the chart's bundled values.yaml, then -f/--values files (later files overriding earlier ones), then --set flags, which always win regardless of where they appear on the command line. So image.tag=2.0 from --set overrides both image.tag: "1.5" from values-a.yaml and image.tag: "1.0" from the chart's default. Option A and B both misstate the precedence order (values.yaml is actually the lowest-precedence source, not the highest, and -f files are overridden by --set, not the reverse). Option D is wrong -- Helm is specifically designed to let the same key be set in multiple layered sources; that's the entire point of the override mechanism, not an error condition.

assessments.prompt: A chart's Chart.yaml has `version: 2.3.0` and `appVersion: 1.4.0`. The chart author fixes a bug in a template (say, a missing label) without changing anything about the application image itself. Which field, if any, should change as a result?
options: Neither field needs to change -- Chart.yaml's version fields are purely decorative and have no bearing on chart behavior.

version should be bumped (e.g., to 2.3.1), since it tracks how many times the chart's own packaging has changed; appVersion should stay at 1.4.0, since it tracks the version of the deployed application, which hasn't changed at all.
appVersion should be bumped instead, since any change to the packaging is considered part of the application's own versioning by Helm.
Both fields must always be incremented together in lockstep, since Helm enforces that version and appVersion stay synchronized.
assessments.explanation: This concept is explicit that version and appVersion are 'deliberately independent, since you can ship a packaging fix without the application itself changing at all, or vice versa.' A template-only bug fix is exactly that case: the chart's own packaging changed, so version should move, while the actual application deployed by the chart is unchanged, so appVersion stays put. Option A dismisses fields that genuinely do communicate meaningful information to chart consumers (e.g., helm search, artifact repositories). Option C reverses which field tracks which concern. Option D invents an enforcement rule Helm doesn't have -- nothing requires these two numbers to move together.

assessments.prompt: A template wraps a resources block in `{{- if .Values.resources }} ... {{- end }}` rather than rendering it unconditionally. What problem does this conditional specifically guard against?
options: It prevents Helm from crashing outright the moment .Values.resources is referenced anywhere in the chart.

It avoids emitting a resources: key with no meaningful content when resources hasn't actually been set for a given install -- rendering it unconditionally regardless of whether the value exists could produce output that's semantically empty or syntactically invalid depending on what follows.
It causes Helm to automatically substitute a hardcoded default resources block whenever the condition evaluates to false.
It's purely a stylistic convention with no effect on whether the rendered YAML is valid either way.
assessments.explanation: The conditional exists precisely because emitting a key like resources: with nothing meaningful underneath it -- which is what happens if resources was never set and the block renders anyway -- can range from harmless to outright invalid YAML depending on the surrounding structure, so gating the whole block on the value actually being present avoids that failure mode entirely. Option A overstates what an unset value would do -- referencing an unset map in a template doesn't crash Helm by itself. Option C invents an automatic substitution behavior the conditional doesn't provide; the else-branch here is simply 'emit nothing.' Option D understates the real, structural effect this conditional has on the rendered output's validity.

assessments.prompt: What do the leading `{{-` and trailing `-}}` whitespace-trim markers actually do in a Go template, and why does this concept treat them as more than a cosmetic detail?
options: They tell the template engine to treat the enclosed expression as a raw string literal instead of evaluating it.

They strip the newline and indentation immediately before/after the tag, preventing stray blank lines from accumulating around conditionals and loops -- and because stray blank lines inside a nested block can shift indentation, this can determine whether the rendered output is even valid YAML, not merely how it looks.
They raise this particular value's precedence above any --set flag supplied later on the command line.
They force the template engine to render the enclosed block as JSON instead of YAML.
assessments.explanation: This concept states this directly: the trim markers strip surrounding whitespace/newlines, which is 'a purely cosmetic-looking detail that actually determines whether the rendered file is even valid YAML, since stray blank lines inside a block scalar can shift indentation in ways that break parsing.' It's a structural correctness mechanism disguised as a formatting nicety. Option A confuses trim markers with an entirely different templating concept (literal-string escaping). Option C invents a connection to Helm's values-precedence system that doesn't exist -- trim markers are purely about template whitespace, unrelated to value resolution order. Option D is false; the trim markers have no bearing on output format.

assessments.prompt: A chart's values.yaml defines `resources: { requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } }`. An override values file sets only `resources.requests.memory: 512Mi`. What does the merged, final value of `resources.requests` end up being?
options: { cpu: 100m, memory: 512Mi } -- the deep merge replaces only the specific key the override sets, preserving cpu from the chart's default since the override never mentioned it.
{ memory: 512Mi } -- specifying any key under requests in an override file replaces the entire requests map wholesale, discarding cpu entirely.
Helm raises an error, since resources.requests is defined in two different sources and can't be automatically reconciled.
{ cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi } -- the override is ignored entirely because it only sets a nested key rather than the whole resources block.
assessments.explanation: This concept is explicit that value merging is 'a deep merge on maps, not a wholesale replacement' -- exactly the scenario given as its own example: overriding only resources.requests.memory keeps cpu: 100m from the chart's default untouched, changing only the specific key the override actually names. Option B describes a shallow/wholesale-replace merge strategy, which is precisely the behavior this concept says Helm does NOT use. Option C invents an error condition; layered value overrides across multiple sources are the entire point of the mechanism, not a conflict. Option D incorrectly claims nested overrides are ignored, when they're exactly what a values override file is designed to express.

assessments.prompt: What is the specific difference between what `helm lint` checks and what `helm template` checks?
options: They're functionally identical; helm lint is simply an older, deprecated alias for helm template.

helm lint runs structural checks against the chart itself (missing required values, malformed chart metadata, YAML that won't parse) without necessarily needing to produce full rendered output; helm template actually renders the chart's templates into final YAML using the given values, letting you inspect exactly what would be sent to the API server.
helm template only works after a chart has already been installed as a live release; helm lint is the only one of the two that works beforehand.
helm lint requires an active connection to a Kubernetes cluster to run, while helm template works entirely offline.
assessments.explanation: This concept describes both commands with distinct roles: helm lint catches structural chart-authoring mistakes (missing values, malformed metadata, unparseable YAML) as a fast first check, while helm template performs the full rendering step and prints the literal output that would be applied, letting you read or diff it before it ever reaches a cluster. Option A collapses two genuinely different commands into one. Option C is backwards and also wrong on the facts -- neither command requires an existing release; both operate on a chart directory directly. Option D is false -- neither command requires a live cluster connection; both are local, offline operations.

assessments.prompt: A teammate maintaining 15 microservices across 4 environments (dev/staging/prod/sandbox) asks why the team should adopt Helm instead of continuing to hand-maintain a separate YAML file per service per environment. Explain the core problem Helm's templating solves, and walk through what changes concretely for a single configuration change (like a new default resource limit) once the switch is made.
assessments.modelAnswer: With 15 services across 4 environments, the team is maintaining something close to 60 independent YAML files that are not actually independent in any meaningful sense -- they're 60 near-copies of a much smaller number of underlying patterns, differing from each other mostly in a handful of parameters like image tag, replica count, and resource limits. Nothing about plain YAML represents that relationship explicitly, so every one of those 60 files has to be kept in sync by hand, and the team's actual failure mode is drift: a resource limit gets bumped in production during an incident and the same fix never makes it into staging, or a new required label gets added to some files but not others, purely because whoever made the edit didn't know to touch every copy. There's also no single artifact representing 'this exact configuration as deployed to prod last week' -- reconstructing what changed between two deploys means diffing raw files by hand across however many of them changed. Helm's templating restructures this entirely: instead of 60 independent files, the team writes one chart per service (15 charts total) containing Go-template-annotated manifests under templates/, plus a small values file per environment holding only the handful of values that actually differ for that environment -- often just image tag, replica count, and a few resource numbers, with everything else falling back to the chart's own defaults. Concretely, rolling out a new default resource limit becomes a single edit to one chart's values.yaml (or, for an environment-specific override, one small values-prod.yaml), rather than 4 separate edits (one per environment) to that one service's files, and any environment that hasn't explicitly overridden that specific value picks up the new default automatically on its next helm upgrade, with zero risk of forgetting to touch one of the copies -- because there are no longer separate copies to forget.

concepts.title: Helm Releases: Install, Upgrade, and Rollback
concepts.description: A Helm release is a named, versioned instance of a chart running in a cluster -- every install and upgrade advances that instance's own revision history, and it's specifically that tracked history, not any cleverness in the Kubernetes API itself, that makes helm rollback a fast, reliable way to undo a bad deploy without reconstructing anything by hand.
learningObjectives: Define what a Helm 'release' is and distinguish it clearly from a 'chart' -- a template versus a specific deployed instance of it.
Use helm install, helm upgrade, helm history, and helm rollback, and describe what each one does to a release's revision history.
Explain where Helm 3 stores release state by default (a Secret per revision) and why that matters for RBAC and cluster inspection.
Explain what --atomic and helm upgrade --install accomplish, and why both matter for CI/CD safety.
Predict what happens if a chart's rendered manifests fail to apply cleanly partway through an upgrade, with and without --atomic.
Explain why uninstalling and reinstalling a release is not equivalent to upgrading it, and what capability is lost by doing so.

sections.heading: A Release Is Not the Same Thing as a Chart
sections.body:
A **chart** is a template: a directory of Go-template-annotated manifests plus a values.yaml, portable and reusable, with no relationship yet to any specific running cluster. A **release** is what you get the moment you actually run `helm install <release-name> <chart>` against a cluster -- a specific, named, running instance of that chart, with a specific set of resolved values, living in a specific namespace, and carrying its own independent revision history from that point forward.

The same chart can back multiple, entirely independent releases simultaneously. Installing `my-app` twice, once as `helm install team-a-web ./my-app -f team-a-values.yaml` and again as `helm install team-b-web ./my-app -f team-b-values.yaml`, produces two releases -- `team-a-web` and `team-b-web` -- each with its own revision history, its own currently-installed values, and its own set of live Kubernetes objects (distinguished from each other by the templated `{{ .Release.Name }}` baked into their names, exactly as in the previous concept's example). Upgrading or rolling back one has zero effect on the other; they only share the chart they both happen to have been installed from, the same way two houses built from the same blueprint share nothing structurally once built.

It's also worth distinguishing this from something covered earlier in this curriculum: a Deployment object has its own rollout history (tracked via ReplicaSets, as covered in Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Rolling Updates). A Helm release's revision history is a *separate, higher-level* concept -- it versions the *entire rendered set of manifests* a chart produces (potentially a Deployment, a Service, a ConfigMap, and more, all at once), not any single object's own history. Rolling back a Helm release can therefore revert several objects' worth of changes together, as one atomic unit, which a single Deployment's own rollout history has no way to express.

sections.heading: Install, Upgrade, Rollback: The Lifecycle Commands
sections.body:
`helm install web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` renders the chart with the merged values and applies the result, creating the release `web` at **revision 1**. `helm upgrade web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` re-renders the chart -- picking up any changes to the chart's templates, to values-prod.yaml, or to any --set flags supplied again -- computes what needs to change against the currently-live objects, applies it, and advances the release to **revision 2**. Every subsequent `helm upgrade` (a new image tag, a scaled replica count, a config change) creates another new revision: 3, 4, 5, and so on, with each one's exact rendered manifests and resolved values retained.

`helm history web` lists every revision with its status (deployed, superseded, failed) and a short description of what changed. `helm rollback web 2` reverts the *live* objects to match revision 2's stored manifests -- but, importantly, this itself creates a **new** revision (say, revision 6, if the release was at revision 5 beforehand) whose *content* matches revision 2, rather than literally rewinding the counter back to 2. The revision number only ever goes up; `helm rollback` is best understood as 'create a new revision using old content,' not 'travel backward in time.'

```bash
helm install web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml     # revision 1
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.5.0    # revision 2
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.6.0    # revision 3 -- bad release
helm rollback web 2                                # revision 4, content == revision 2
helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      CHART           APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.4.0        Install complete
# 2         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.5.0        Upgrade complete
# 3         superseded  my-app-0.1.0    1.6.0        Upgrade complete
# 4         deployed    my-app-0.1.0    1.5.0        Rollback to 2
```

sections.heading: Where Release State Actually Lives
sections.body:
By default, Helm 3 records each release revision as a **Secret** object in the release's own namespace, conventionally named `sh.helm.release.v1.<release-name>.v<revision>` -- one Secret per revision, containing the rendered manifests and resolved values (compressed and base64-encoded) as its payload. `kubectl get secrets -n <namespace> -l owner=helm` lists them directly, and this is worth internalizing for two concrete reasons.

First, because it's stored as a Secret specifically (not a ConfigMap), the exact same facts from the ConfigMaps and Secrets concept apply here: this content is base64-encoded, not encrypted, and RBAC controlling who can read Secret objects in a namespace is therefore also, incidentally, controlling who can read Helm's own release history and resolved values for that namespace -- including anything sensitive that was passed in via `--set` or a values file. A user without permission to read Secrets in a namespace will find `helm history`/`helm get values` failing or coming back empty against that namespace, even if they can otherwise see the Deployments and Services that release created.

Second, these revision Secrets accumulate over time and are not deleted automatically as a release keeps getting upgraded -- `--history-max` (settable per install/upgrade, defaulting to 10) caps how many old revisions Helm retains before pruning the oldest. Retaining fewer revisions saves a small amount of etcd storage but also limits how far back `helm rollback` can reach, since a pruned revision's manifests are simply gone.

sections.heading: Atomic Upgrades and CI/CD Safety
sections.body:
By default, if a `helm upgrade` applies its rendered manifests but one of the resulting objects then fails to actually become healthy -- a new Pod template that never passes readiness, a rollout that stalls -- Helm itself doesn't necessarily notice or react. The release can be left in a state where new objects were created but the rollout never actually finished, and nothing automatically restores the previous good state; a human has to notice and run `helm rollback` manually.

`--atomic` changes this: it instructs Helm to wait for the upgrade's resources to actually become ready (implying `--wait`), and if that doesn't happen within the timeout, to automatically roll back to the release's previous successful revision on its own, with no manual intervention required. This is precisely the property a CI/CD pipeline needs, because it converts 'a bad deploy silently leaves the cluster in a half-upgraded, degraded state until someone notices' into 'a bad deploy self-heals back to the last known-good revision within the pipeline's own deploy step, and the pipeline can simply fail loudly if that self-heal itself fails.'

```bash
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=broken-tag --atomic --timeout 5m
# Error: UPGRADE FAILED: timed out waiting for the condition
# (release automatically rolled back to the previous revision)
```

Separately, `helm upgrade --install` (often written `upgrade -i`) is the idiomatic command for a CI pipeline's deploy step specifically because it removes the need for the pipeline to branch on 'does this release already exist yet or not' -- it upgrades the release if it's already installed, or performs a first-time install if it isn't, with a single command covering both the very first deploy and every deploy after it.

sections.heading: Why Reinstalling Is Not the Same as Upgrading
sections.body:
It's tempting, when an upgrade seems stuck or confusing, to simply `helm uninstall web` and then `helm install web ./my-app` fresh. This works, in the narrow sense that the application ends up running again -- but it throws away something real: the entire revision history built up by every prior install and upgrade is gone, along with the ability to `helm rollback` to any of those earlier states, because uninstalling deletes the release's tracked Secrets entirely, not just the live application objects.

There's also a concrete availability cost: uninstall-then-install is a delete-everything-then-create-everything-fresh sequence, with a real gap in between where none of the release's objects exist at all -- functionally similar to the `Recreate` deployment strategy's outage window covered earlier in this curriculum, rather than the gradual, overlapping transition a normal `helm upgrade` (which itself just drives an ordinary Kubernetes rolling update under the hood, assuming the underlying Deployment uses `RollingUpdate`) produces. Reinstalling should be reserved for genuinely broken situations -- a release stuck in a state no upgrade or rollback can recover from -- not treated as a routine alternative to `helm upgrade` for shipping a normal change.

examples.title: A Full Install-Upgrade-Rollback Cycle
examples.code:
helm install web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.0.0
# NAME: web
# LAST DEPLOYED: ...
# STATUS: deployed
# REVISION: 1

helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.1.0
# REVISION: 2

helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  1.0.0        Install complete
# 2         deployed    1.1.0        Upgrade complete

helm rollback web 1
# Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!

helm history web
# REVISION  STATUS      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
# 1         superseded  1.0.0        Install complete
# 2         superseded  1.1.0        Upgrade complete
# 3         deployed    1.0.0        Rollback to 1
examples.explanation: Notice the final `helm history` output: there is no revision that got deleted or rewound. Revision 3 exists as a brand-new entry whose content matches revision 1's (image tag 1.0.0), and it's revision 3 -- not revision 1 -- that now shows STATUS: deployed. This is the concrete proof that helm rollback always moves the revision counter forward; 'rolling back' describes the effect on the live objects' content, not any literal reversal of the release's own version number. A second `helm rollback web 2` from this point would create revision 4 with image tag 1.1.0's content, and so on -- the history only ever grows.

examples.title: Inspecting Release State as Secrets
examples.code:
kubectl get secrets -n default -l owner=helm
# NAME                          TYPE                 AGE
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v1     helm.sh/release.v1   14m
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v2     helm.sh/release.v1   9m
# sh.helm.release.v1.web.v3     helm.sh/release.v1   1m

kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n default --as=system:serviceaccount:default:ci-deployer
# no

helm history web --namespace default
# Error: release: not found
# (the ci-deployer identity can't read the release Secrets, so Helm can't see the history either)
examples.explanation: Each revision from the previous example produced its own Secret object, named with the release name and revision number embedded directly -- exactly the storage mechanism described in this concept. The second block demonstrates the RBAC consequence directly: a ServiceAccount denied `get` on Secrets in this namespace can't read Helm's own release history either, even though that ServiceAccount might have full permission to read the Deployments and Services the release actually created -- because from Helm's point of view, the release's bookkeeping IS a Secret, subject to exactly the same access control as any other Secret in the namespace, no more and no less.

examples.title: --atomic Catching a Broken Upgrade
examples.code:
# Without --atomic: a broken upgrade is applied and left half-done
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=typo-tag
# Release "web" has been upgraded. Happy Helming!
# (but the new Pods are stuck in ImagePullBackOff -- nobody has rolled anything back)

kubectl get pods -l app=web
# web-8a1e2f4c3-h9z1x   0/1   ImagePullBackOff

# With --atomic: the same broken upgrade self-heals
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=typo-tag --atomic --timeout 3m
# Error: UPGRADE FAILED: release web failed, and has been rolled back due to atomic being set: timed out waiting for the condition

helm history web
# (current revision's content still matches the last GOOD image tag -- unaffected by the failed attempt)
examples.explanation: Without --atomic, `helm upgrade` reports success as soon as it finishes applying the rendered manifests -- it does not, by itself, wait around to confirm the new Pods actually become healthy, so a broken image tag leaves the cluster in a half-upgraded state (old Pods possibly already scaled down, new Pods stuck) with no automatic correction. With --atomic, Helm waits for readiness up to --timeout and, on failure, automatically issues the equivalent of a rollback to the previous good revision on its own -- the exact same underlying mechanism as a manual `helm rollback`, just triggered automatically as part of the failed upgrade attempt, which is precisely why CI/CD pipelines deploying via Helm should default to including --atomic on every upgrade rather than treating it as optional.

misconceptions.description: helm rollback web 2 restores revision 2 as the current revision, so the release's revision counter goes back down to 2 and the next upgrade after that would become revision 3.
misconceptions.clarification: The revision counter only ever increases. Rolling back to revision 2 from a release currently at revision 5 creates a brand-new revision 6, whose rendered manifests and values happen to match what revision 2 had -- it does not delete revisions 3, 4, or 5, and it does not make revision 2 itself the current one again. The next upgrade after this rollback would become revision 7, not revision 3. helm history after any rollback will always show every revision that ever existed, including the rollback itself as a new entry, never a shortened or rewound list.

misconceptions.description: Once a release is installed, the chart's source directory (or its entry in a local/remote chart repository) needs to stay available, since Kubernetes has to keep referring back to it to keep the release's objects running.
misconceptions.clarification: Once helm install or upgrade has applied the rendered manifests, the resulting Kubernetes objects (Deployments, Services, and so on) are ordinary, independent objects living in etcd -- nothing about their continued operation depends on the chart's source files existing anywhere anymore, any more than a kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml Deployment depends on deployment.yaml still being on disk. The chart's source (and Helm's own stored copy of the exact manifests/values used, inside the release's revision Secret) is only needed again the next time you run a Helm command against that release -- another upgrade, a rollback, or an uninstall -- not for the objects to keep functioning in between.

exercises.prompt: A release goes through: install (rev 1, tag=1.0), upgrade (rev 2, tag=1.1), upgrade (rev 3, tag=1.2), then `helm rollback web 1`. What revision number is now marked 'deployed', and what image tag do the live Pods actually run?
exercises.code:
helm install web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.0
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.1
helm upgrade web ./my-app --set image.tag=1.2
helm rollback web 1
helm history web   # ?
hints: Rolling back doesn't erase or reuse an old revision number -- it always creates a new one on top of whatever the release is currently at.
The release was at revision 3 right before the rollback command ran. What's the next available revision number after 3?
The NEW revision's CONTENT (image tag) comes from whichever old revision you rolled back to -- track those two things (revision number vs. content) separately.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Revision 4 is now marked 'deployed', and the live Pods run image tag 1.0 -- the content of revision 1, copied forward into a brand-new revision 4, rather than revision 1 itself becoming current again.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Before the rollback, the release has three revisions: 1 (tag 1.0), 2 (tag 1.1), 3 (tag 1.2, currently deployed). helm rollback web 1 does not resurrect revision 1 as-is or delete revisions 2 and 3 -- it creates a new revision, 4, whose rendered manifests and values are copied from revision 1's stored state, and marks that new revision 4 as deployed. So the answer has two independent parts: the revision NUMBER that's now current is 4 (the counter only ever climbs), while the actual running CONTENT (image tag 1.0) matches revision 1's, because that's what was rolled back to. A subsequent helm history web would show four entries total: 1, 2, 3 all superseded, and 4 deployed with a description like 'Rollback to 1'.

exercises.prompt: This CI deploy script fails every run after the very first one, with 'Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: cannot re-use a name that is still in use.' The team wants every merge to main to deploy the latest image, whether or not this is the first deploy ever. Find and fix the bug.
hints: helm install has no notion of 'update if it already exists' -- what verb does Helm provide specifically for a release that might already be installed?
There's a single Helm command that installs a release if it doesn't exist yet, or upgrades it if it does, without the script needing to check which case it's in.
The fix is a one-word change to the command being run, not a change to any of the flags.
exercises.solutionExplanation: helm install is a one-time-only operation -- calling it again against a release name that already exists fails outright with exactly the error shown, mirroring how kubectl create behaves against an object that already exists. helm upgrade --install (the --install flag, often abbreviated -i) is designed specifically for this repeated-deploy-from-CI scenario: it upgrades the release if web already exists, or performs a first-time install if it doesn't, so the same command works correctly on the very first deploy and every deploy after it, with no branching logic needed in the script at all. Adding --atomic --timeout 5m on top (not strictly required to fix the reported error, but a meaningful CI/CD safety improvement covered in this concept) also ensures a broken image tag self-heals back to the previous good revision automatically rather than leaving a half-upgraded release in place.

assessments.prompt: By default, where does Helm 3 store the rendered manifests and resolved values for each release revision?
options: In a dedicated Tiller server component running inside the cluster.
In a Secret object per revision, in the release's own namespace, subject to the same RBAC rules as any other Secret.
Only locally, in a hidden directory on the machine that ran the helm command.
In a ConfigMap per release, shared across all of that release's revisions.
assessments.explanation: Helm 3 stores each revision's rendered manifests and values as a Secret object (named sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>) in the release's namespace -- one Secret per revision, not per release, and governed by ordinary Kubernetes RBAC exactly like any other Secret. Option A describes Helm 2's architecture; Tiller was removed entirely in Helm 3, which talks to the Kubernetes API directly using the user's own credentials. Option C is false -- the whole point of storing state in-cluster is that helm history/rollback work from any machine with cluster access, not just the one that ran the original install. Option D is wrong on both counts: it's a Secret, not a ConfigMap, and there's one per revision, not one shared across all revisions of a release.

assessments.prompt: The same chart `my-app` is installed twice: once as release `team-a-web` and once as release `team-b-web`, each with its own values file. `team-a-web` is then rolled back to an earlier revision. What happens to `team-b-web` as a result?
options: team-b-web is also rolled back automatically, since both releases share the same underlying chart and Helm keeps sibling releases derived from it synchronized.

Nothing happens to team-b-web at all -- each release has its own independent revision history and its own live objects; the two releases only share the chart template they both happened to be installed from, nothing more.
team-b-web's own revision counter resets to 1, since rolling back any release derived from a shared chart resets version tracking cluster-wide.
Helm refuses to roll back team-a-web at all unless team-b-web is rolled back in the same operation.
assessments.explanation: This concept is explicit that 'upgrading or rolling back one has zero effect on the other; they only share the chart they both happen to have been installed from, the same way two houses built from the same blueprint share nothing structurally once built.' Each release's revision history, live objects, and current values are entirely independent bookkeeping, keyed by release name. Options A, C, and D all invent a cross-release coupling that doesn't exist in Helm's actual design -- releases are deliberately isolated from one another even when derived from the same chart source.

assessments.prompt: A chart's templates include a Deployment, a Service, and a ConfigMap. After several `helm upgrade` calls, the team runs `helm rollback web 2`. How does this differ from running `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` directly?
options: They're functionally identical -- helm rollback simply calls kubectl rollout undo internally on every Deployment in the chart, and does nothing else.

helm rollback reverts the entire rendered set of objects the chart produces -- the Deployment, the Service, and the ConfigMap together, as one unit -- based on the release's own higher-level revision history, whereas kubectl rollout undo only reverts that one specific Deployment's own rollout history, with no awareness of the Service or ConfigMap at all.
kubectl rollout undo actually reverts more objects overall than helm rollback, since it acts directly on the cluster rather than going through Helm's abstraction layer.
Neither command is capable of acting on more than one object per invocation; both require being run separately against each object in the chart.
assessments.explanation: This concept draws this distinction directly: a Helm release's revision history is 'a separate, higher-level concept -- it versions the entire rendered set of manifests a chart produces ... not any single object's own history,' while a Deployment's own rollout history (from the Deployments concept) covers only that one object. Rolling back a release can therefore revert several objects together as one atomic unit, something a single Deployment's rollout history has no way to express on its own. Option A wildly understates what helm rollback actually reverts. Option C reverses which mechanism has the broader scope. Option D is false for helm rollback specifically, which is precisely what lets it act on multiple objects in one command.

assessments.prompt: A release has been upgraded 15 times under the default `--history-max` setting of 10. Can `helm rollback web 2` still succeed?
options: Yes, always -- history-max only limits how many revisions helm history displays on screen; it never actually deletes any revision's underlying stored data.

Not necessarily -- history-max caps how many old revisions Helm actually retains before pruning the oldest ones, so if revision 2 has already been pruned to stay within the limit of 10, its stored manifests are simply gone and a rollback to it can no longer succeed.
Yes, because Helm always guarantees revision 1 and every subsequent even-numbered revision are retained regardless of history-max.
No -- rollback is only ever possible to the single immediately preceding revision, regardless of what history-max is set to.
assessments.explanation: This concept states plainly that revision Secrets 'accumulate over time and are not deleted automatically,' and that history-max 'caps how many old revisions Helm retains before pruning the oldest' -- with the direct consequence that 'retaining fewer revisions ... limits how far back helm rollback can reach, since a pruned revision's manifests are simply gone.' With 15 upgrades and a cap of 10, early revisions (potentially including revision 2) may already have been pruned, making that specific rollback target unavailable. Option A misdescribes history-max as a display-only limit rather than an actual retention/pruning policy. Option C invents an even/odd retention guarantee that doesn't exist. Option D is false -- helm rollback can target any retained revision, not just the immediately preceding one.

assessments.prompt: A CI pipeline's very first deploy of a brand-new release runs `helm upgrade web ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml` (without the --install flag). What happens?
options: It succeeds and performs a first-time install automatically, since helm upgrade silently falls back to install behavior whenever no prior release exists.

It fails, because there is no existing release named web yet for helm upgrade to act on -- helm upgrade expects a release to already exist, which is exactly the gap the --install flag exists to close.
It succeeds, but creates the release starting at revision number 0 instead of 1, to signal that it took the upgrade code path.
It always succeeds identically to helm install, since upgrade and install have been fully interchangeable commands since Helm 3.
assessments.explanation: helm upgrade on its own has no built-in fallback for a nonexistent release -- it's designed to act on a release that's already installed. This concept describes helm upgrade --install as the command specifically designed to remove the need for a pipeline to branch on 'does this release already exist yet,' which only makes sense if plain helm upgrade doesn't already handle that case on its own. Option A invents exactly the fallback behavior that --install is needed to add. Option C invents a nonstandard revision-numbering behavior. Option D is false -- if upgrade and install were fully interchangeable, there would be no reason for --install to exist as a distinct, separately documented flag.

assessments.prompt: A team decides that instead of debugging a confusing `helm upgrade`, they'll just run `helm uninstall web` followed by `helm install web ./my-app`. Besides the brief availability gap, what specific capability do they lose by doing this instead of fixing the upgrade?
options: Nothing meaningful -- uninstalling and reinstalling preserves the release's revision history internally, so helm rollback to any earlier revision still works afterward.

The entire revision history built up by every prior install and upgrade, since uninstalling deletes the release's tracked revision Secrets entirely -- meaning helm rollback can no longer reach any of those earlier states once the fresh install starts a brand-new history at revision 1.
Only the single most recent revision is lost; every earlier revision remains rollback-able after the reinstall completes.
The application's persistent data is always deleted as a direct, guaranteed consequence of running helm uninstall, regardless of what storage mechanism backs it.
assessments.explanation: This concept is direct about the real cost: 'uninstalling deletes the release's tracked Secrets entirely, not just the live application objects,' so the entire revision history -- and the ability to roll back to any of those earlier states -- is gone, with the fresh install starting over at revision 1. Option A claims the opposite of what actually happens. Option C understates the loss, which is total, not limited to the most recent revision. Option D overclaims a guaranteed data-deletion behavior; whether persistent data survives depends on separate mechanisms (like a PVC's reclaim policy from the Storage concept), not on helm uninstall itself universally destroying it.

assessments.prompt: Explain what --atomic changes about how helm upgrade handles a broken deploy, and why a CI/CD pipeline that deploys via Helm should treat it as close to mandatory rather than optional.
assessments.modelAnswer: Without --atomic, helm upgrade's job ends the moment it has successfully applied the newly rendered manifests to the cluster -- it does not wait around afterward to confirm that the resulting objects actually become healthy. This means a broken change (a bad image tag, a misconfigured probe, anything that prevents the new Pods from ever becoming Ready) can be 'successfully' applied by Helm's own accounting, while the cluster is left in a genuinely degraded, half-upgraded state: possibly some old Pods already scaled down, new Pods stuck failing to start, and nothing automatically correcting any of it until a human notices and manually runs helm rollback. --atomic changes this contract: it makes helm upgrade implicitly wait (the same as passing --wait) for the upgraded resources to actually reach a healthy state within the given --timeout, and if that doesn't happen, it automatically performs the equivalent of a rollback to the release's previous successful revision on its own, with the helm upgrade command itself then reporting a clear failure rather than a false success. For a CI/CD pipeline specifically, this distinction is the difference between 'a bad deploy silently degrades production until someone happens to notice, potentially minutes or hours later' and 'a bad deploy is caught and reverted within the pipeline's own deploy step, and the pipeline's build simply goes red, immediately and unambiguously, exactly where the mistake was introduced.' Since the whole premise of automated deployment is that changes ship without a human watching every single one in real time, --atomic is effectively supplying the safety net that a human operator would otherwise have needed to provide by hand -- which is precisely why it's considered close to mandatory rather than a nice-to-have flag.
